title: “GIVE, AND IT WILL BE GIVEN TO YOU” — THE VERSE WE TURNED INTO A MONEY PROMISE WHILE MISSING THE HEART OF JESUS
paragraphs: “GIVE, AND IT WILL BE GIVEN TO YOU” — THE VERSE WE TURNED INTO A MONEY PROMISE WHILE MISSING THE HEART OF JESUS

What if one of the most quoted promises about giving was never meant to make you rich, but to expose what bitterness, unforgiveness, fear, and selfishness have been doing to your soul? The truth behind Luke 6:38 may change how you give, how you forgive, how you treat people, and how you understand the grace of God.
There is something deeply unsettling about a Bible verse that sounds beautiful until you discover what Jesus was actually saying.
You have probably heard it before.
“Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over…” — Luke 6:38 (KJV)
Maybe you heard it during an offering.
Maybe someone quoted it while encouraging you to sow a financial seed.
Maybe you were struggling to pay your bills, and somebody told you that if you gave enough money, God would give you even more in return.
And perhaps you gave.
Not because you had plenty.
But because you were desperate.

You gave while worrying about the electricity bill. You gave while wondering how you would buy groceries. You gave with trembling hands and a heart whispering, “Lord, please. I need You to come through for me.”
Then the following morning came.
The bills were still there.
Your bank account had not miraculously multiplied.
And somewhere in the silence, a painful question began forming.
“Did I not have enough faith?”
But what if the problem was never the size of your faith?
What if someone had taken a beautiful teaching from Jesus, pulled it away from its original context, and turned it into a financial formula that Christ never promised?
And what if the true meaning is far more confronting, far more beautiful, and far more transformative than anything money could purchase?
Because when Jesus said, “Give, and it will be given to you,” He was speaking about something that reaches into the darkest corners of the human heart.
Something we would rather avoid.
Something that can expose a person who gives generously at church but refuses to forgive someone at home.
And to understand it, we need to go back to the words Jesus spoke before that famous verse.
Not merely the words we like to quote.
The words we often leave behind.
In Luke 6:27, Jesus says something almost offensive to our wounded human nature:
“But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you.”
Read that again.
Love your enemies.
Not merely tolerate them.
Not secretly hope they experience the consequences of what they did to you.
Love them.
Then Jesus continues.
“Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.” — Luke 6:28 (KJV)
Can you imagine hearing that when someone has betrayed your trust?
When a friend has damaged your reputation?
When someone you helped financially suddenly acts as though you never existed?
When a family member has wounded you so deeply that even hearing their name makes your chest tighten?
Jesus does not pretend those wounds are imaginary.
He does not call evil good.
He does not command you to remain in an abusive situation or surrender wise boundaries.
But He does confront something dangerous that can happen inside us after we have been hurt.
We can begin believing that because someone treated us without mercy, we are entitled to live without mercy toward them.
And slowly, the wound becomes our identity.
We rehearse conversations that ended years ago.
We prepare speeches for arguments that may never happen.
We remember every offense with astonishing accuracy while struggling to remember the grace that has carried us through our own failures.
Then Jesus speaks again.
“Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.” — Luke 6:36 (KJV)
There it is.
The heartbeat of the passage.
Mercy.
And then comes Luke 6:37:
“Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.”
Only after these words does Jesus say:
“Give, and it shall be given unto you.”
Do you see what happens when we stop isolating verse 38 from everything surrounding it?
Jesus has been talking about loving enemies, blessing those who mistreat us, showing mercy, refusing a condemning spirit, and extending forgiveness.
Then He speaks about giving.
The immediate context is not a fundraising campaign.
It is the character of a person being transformed by the mercy of God.
And that changes everything.
The Greek text of Luke 6:38 begins:
Δίδοτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν
Didote, kai dothēsetai hymin.
A faithful translation is:
“Give, and it will be given to you.”
The word δίδοτε (didote) comes from the Greek verb didōmi, meaning “to give.” Here it is a present-tense imperative, calling Jesus' hearers to practice giving.
The verb itself does not mean “give money.”
Its meaning depends on the context.
And in this context, Jesus is describing a life of generous mercy.
He continues with the imagery:
μέτρον καλὸν πεπιεσμένον σεσαλευμένον ὑπερεκχυννόμενον
Metron kalon pepiesmenon sesaleumenon hyperekchynnomenon.
A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, overflowing.
Picture an ancient marketplace.
A merchant is measuring grain into a container.
Instead of leaving empty spaces, the grain is pressed down and shaken so that more can fit. The measure is filled until it overflows.
Jesus uses this vivid picture to communicate abundance.
But notice what He does not say.
He does not say that every financial gift guarantees a larger financial payment.
He does not promise that giving a certain amount to a religious organization will produce a particular return on investment.
He does not turn generosity into a technique for controlling God's provision.
Instead, He concludes:
“For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.” — Luke 6:38 (KJV)
The measure you use matters.
The mercy you extend matters.
The generosity of your heart matters.
The way you treat others matters.
And while the promise includes receiving, Jesus does not specify that every act of generosity will be repaid with money, nor does He establish a predictable timetable for receiving.
This is not a denial of God's provision.
It is a refusal to reduce God's provision to a transaction.
And that distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because some of the most generous people you will ever meet are not wealthy.
Some give while living with very little.
Some have spent years caring for sick relatives, feeding hungry neighbors, comforting grieving friends, and quietly helping people who will never repay them.
Their generosity may never make them famous.
It may never produce a large bank balance.
But it is not invisible to God.
Remember the poor widow in Mark 12:41–44?
Jesus watched people placing money into the temple treasury.
Many wealthy people gave large amounts.
Then a poor widow came and offered two small copper coins.
Jesus called His disciples' attention to her.
Not because her offering was financially impressive.
But because He saw the sacrifice that others could not see.
She had given out of her poverty.
Notice something important.
Jesus honored her giving, but the passage does not say that she walked home wealthy afterward.
There is no recorded financial multiplication.
No guaranteed prosperity formula.
No announcement that her two coins would become two thousand.
The point is that Jesus sees the heart and the cost of what is given.
And that should both comfort and challenge us.
Because perhaps you have been measuring your spiritual worth by what you can afford to give.
Perhaps you feel ashamed because someone else can contribute more.
Perhaps you have quietly wondered whether God loves financially successful believers more than those who are barely surviving.
Hear this clearly.
Your bank balance is not the measure of God's love for you.
The cross is where the love of God is displayed with unmistakable clarity.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8 (KJV)
Christ did not wait until you became financially useful.
He did not ask whether you could afford a monthly contribution before offering you salvation.
He loved you while you were still a sinner.
He gave Himself for you.
And that brings us to the most breathtaking act of giving in the entire Bible.
Not the widow's coins.
Not a wealthy man's donation.
Not an offering collected in a church service.
But the Son of God giving His life for sinners.
Jesus was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
And while He hung upon the cross, surrounded by cruelty, He prayed:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” — Luke 23:34 (KJV)
There, in the darkest moment of human injustice, we see the mercy Jesus had been teaching.
The One who commanded us to love our enemies demonstrated love toward His enemies.
The One who taught us to pray for those who mistreat us prayed for those involved in His crucifixion.
The One who called us to mercy opened the way for guilty people to receive forgiveness.
This is the Gospel.
Not that we can purchase God's favor through generosity.
But that Jesus Christ has accomplished what our money, morality, religious activity, and good intentions could never accomplish.
Salvation is not for sale.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Grace is a gift.
Forgiveness is found in Christ.
And genuine faith produces a transformed life.
That transformation includes how we handle money.
But it reaches much further.
It reaches the dinner table where a husband and wife have stopped speaking kindly to one another.
It reaches the family gathering where an old betrayal is still quietly controlling the atmosphere.
It reaches the workplace where jealousy has made someone incapable of celebrating another person's success.
It reaches the church where someone can lift both hands in worship while holding bitterness toward the person sitting three rows away.
It reaches the private thoughts we never post online.
The resentments we disguise as discernment.
The pride we call standards.
The grudges we have carried for so long that they now feel like part of our personality.
And Jesus asks us to surrender all of it to Him.
Not because forgiveness is easy.
Not because injustice does not matter.
Not because reconciliation is always safe or immediately possible.
But because the mercy of God is too glorious to receive and then deliberately refuse to reflect.
Imagine a man who has been carrying bitterness against his father for twenty years.
He remembers the shouting.
The broken promises.
The birthdays that passed without a phone call.
He remembers watching other children run into their fathers' arms while wondering why his own father seemed incapable of loving him.
Now he is grown.
He has children of his own.
He attends church.
He gives offerings.
He knows the worship songs.
But whenever his father's name is mentioned, something inside him hardens.
One evening, he opens his Bible to Luke 6.
He reads about loving enemies.
Praying for those who mistreat us.
Being merciful.
Forgiving.
Giving.
And for the first time, he realizes that the generosity Jesus is describing cannot be confined to an offering envelope.
His money has been moving.
But his mercy has been standing still.
Perhaps he begins to pray.
Not a polished prayer.
Not a prayer that sounds impressive in a church microphone.
Just a broken whisper.
“Jesus, I don't know how to forgive him. I don't even know if I want to. But I don't want this bitterness to keep ruling my life. Please help me.”
Nothing dramatic may happen immediately.
His father may never apologize.
Trust may not be restored.
Healthy boundaries may remain necessary.
But something sacred has begun.
He is no longer pretending the bitterness is harmless.
He is bringing it into the presence of Christ.
And perhaps that is where someone reading this article finds themselves today.
You are not struggling to give money.
You are struggling to give mercy.
You are struggling to release the desire to see someone suffer as much as they made you suffer.
You are struggling to stop condemning yourself for a past that Jesus has already called you to bring into the light.
You are struggling to believe that the same grace you celebrate in worship could reach the parts of your story that still make you ashamed.
And maybe the hardest person for you to stop condemning is the person staring back at you in the mirror.
You remember who you were.
What you did.
What you said.
The people you hurt.
The opportunities you wasted.
The promises you made to God and broke.
You know the scandal of your own story.
But listen.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Repentance does not mean pretending the past never happened.
It means turning from sin toward the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
And when you belong to Christ, your worst chapter does not have to become your final identity.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because grace excuses rebellion.
But because Jesus rewrites everything through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and the transforming power of His Gospel.
Now consider another important question.
If Luke 6:38 is primarily about the generous mercy Jesus calls us to practice, does that mean financial giving is unbiblical?
Absolutely not.
Scripture teaches financial generosity clearly.
But we must build that teaching on passages that actually address it.
In 2 Corinthians 9, the apostle Paul encourages believers to contribute to a collection for Christians in need.
He writes:
Look closely.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
Not under compulsion.
Giving is meant to be willing and sincere.
Paul also teaches that God is able to provide for believers so that they may abound in good works (2 Corinthians 9:8).
But the passage is not a guarantee that every donation will produce personal wealth.
In fact, the chapter emphasizes generosity, righteousness, thanksgiving to God, and meeting the needs of others.
And in 2 Corinthians 8:12, Paul makes a statement that every financially struggling believer deserves to hear:
“For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.”
According to what a person has.
Not what they do not have.
God does not require you to pretend you possess resources that you do not possess.
In the same collection, Paul explains that he does not intend for others to be relieved while the givers themselves are burdened, but seeks fairness (2 Corinthians 8:13–14).
That matters.
Because a faithful Christian appeal for financial support should never be built on guilt, panic, shame, or the suggestion that God will punish someone for being unable to contribute.
Giving is worship when it flows from faith and love.
It becomes spiritually dangerous when it is used to manipulate people.
There is also an important distinction between tithes, offerings, and voluntary support for a Christian ministry.

In the Old Testament, Israel's tithing obligations belonged to the covenant life and worship of the nation, with provisions connected to the Levites, religious observances, and care for vulnerable people.
In the New Testament, believers are called to generous, willing, proportionate, and responsible giving.
Christians and church traditions differ on whether the ten-percent tithe remains a binding standard for Christians today.
What we can say clearly is that Scripture supports caring for those in need and materially supporting faithful Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 speaks about sharing good things with those who teach the Word.
First Corinthians 9:14 affirms the legitimacy of Gospel workers receiving support through Gospel ministry.
First Timothy 5:17–18 also addresses honoring and supporting faithful church elders.
It can be a voluntary ministry contribution.
It can be a meaningful offering of support.
It can help sustain the creation and distribution of biblical resources.
But it is not a payment for grace.
And it is not the price of God's blessing.
Not as someone trying to extract money from your faith.
But as someone inviting you to consider what it means to help make faithful, Christ-centered teaching accessible to people who desperately need it.
Somewhere tonight, there may be a believer who is close to giving up.
Someone who still believes in God but has stopped believing that God could possibly want someone like them.
Someone who has been quietly battling temptation, loneliness, grief, spiritual exhaustion, or overwhelming guilt.
Someone who has not opened a Bible in months because every time they try, they remember how far they have wandered.
And perhaps one article about the mercy of Jesus could encourage that person to open Scripture again.
Perhaps one devotional could help someone pray honestly for the first time in years.
Perhaps one Gospel-centered resource could help a struggling believer understand repentance without falling into despair.
We cannot promise what God will do through any particular post, book, or message.
Only the Lord knows the hearts He will reach.
But we can faithfully sow the Word.
We can make biblical resources available.
We can point people to Christ.
And we can invite others to participate in that work.
That is part of the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
These resources are not intended to replace Scripture, prayer, or the fellowship and accountability of a faithful local church.
They are meant to encourage deeper study, spiritual growth, and everyday discipleship.
And making resources available takes ongoing time, work, and support.
Not because God needs your money to accomplish His purposes.
He does not.
And certainly not because giving to Gospel Warrior guarantees financial prosperity.
But because supporting sound biblical teaching can be one meaningful expression of Christian generosity when done willingly, wisely, and with a sincere desire to glorify God.
Let it be a decision made in freedom rather than pressure.
Let it be part of your wider commitment to generosity, not a substitute for caring for your household, supporting your local church, or helping people in need.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, encouragement for personal devotion, or meaningful gifts for someone you love.
It will be the opportunity to help keep Christ-centered encouragement and biblical teaching available to others.
You are not less faithful.
You are not less welcome.
You are not less valuable to this ministry.
You can still help.
You can pray.
You can encourage someone.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to perform spirituality for an audience.
But because sometimes speaking truthfully about what God is showing us can encourage another person to stop hiding.
“Jesus, teach me to forgive.”
Maybe it is:
“Pray for me. I've been carrying bitterness for years.”
Maybe it is:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or perhaps:
“Lord, teach me to give without expecting anything in return.”
You do not need to share private details you are not ready to reveal.
But if this message has brought something to the surface, consider leaving a comment that reflects your prayer or testimony.
Because someone reading the comments may be struggling with the very thing you have finally found the courage to bring before Christ.
And sometimes a simple testimony can remind another person that they are not alone in the fight of faith.
Now, before we finish, I want you to return to Luke 6:38 one more time.
But this time, do not picture an offering basket.
Picture the person who wounded you.
Picture the person you have been avoiding.
Picture the stranger who cannot repay your kindness.
Picture the struggling believer who needs encouragement more than criticism.
Picture the person who has failed and is wondering whether repentance and restoration are still possible.
Picture your own heart.
And listen again to Jesus.
“Give, and it shall be given unto you…”
What if today He is calling you to give mercy where you have been withholding it?
What if He is calling you to give compassion where you have been quick to condemn?
What if He is calling you to give forgiveness while wisely maintaining boundaries?
What if He is calling you to give financial help to someone who cannot possibly repay you?
What if He is calling you to give your time, your attention, your prayers, or your encouragement?
What if He is calling you to stop treating generosity as a strategy for getting something and begin seeing it as the fruit of belonging to Someone?
Because the greatest gift God has given us is not a financial breakthrough.
It is Jesus Christ.
And the greatest miracle is not that money can change hands.
It is that the Gospel can change hearts.
A selfish person can learn generosity.
A bitter person can learn mercy.
A proud person can learn humility.
A guilty sinner can receive forgiveness through Christ.
A spiritually exhausted believer can find fresh strength in the grace of God.
And a life marked by sin, shame, and brokenness can become a testimony to the redeeming power of Jesus.
That is what we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the old story never happened.
But by entering the story with truth, mercy, forgiveness, and resurrection power.
So give.
Give wisely.
Give willingly.
Give compassionately.
Give financially when you are able and led by biblical conviction.
Give mercy because you have received mercy.
Give forgiveness because Christ has forgiven you, remembering that forgiveness and restored trust are not always the same thing.
Give without turning God into a debtor.
Give without imagining you can purchase His favor.
And when you have nothing material to offer, remember that you can still pray, encourage, love, and bear witness to the Gospel.
Do not confuse the size of your gift with the size of your faith.
Do not confuse material abundance with spiritual maturity.
Do not confuse financial hardship with divine rejection.
And never forget that the hands of Jesus were not stretched out on the cross to collect a payment from you.
They were pierced as He gave Himself for sinners.
That is the generosity that changes everything.
Your prayers, your shares, your encouragement, and your willing support can all play a part in helping this message reach beyond the people who already know where to look.
But above everything else, let your response begin with Christ.
Because the goal is not merely to become a better giver.
It is to become more like the Savior who gave Himself for us.
And perhaps the prayer we need most tonight is not, “Lord, how much will You give me if I give?”
Perhaps it is:

“Lord Jesus, You have already shown me mercy I could never earn. Forgive my selfishness. Heal what bitterness has damaged. Teach me to love people truthfully, generously, and wisely. Make my life a reflection of Your grace. And whether I have much or little, let everything I offer bring glory to You.”
Amen.
You may spend your whole life asking God to fill your hands, while Jesus is patiently teaching your heart how to open them.
